fieldissues.issue: “Election Interference” and “Democratic Institution Undermining” frame a poll about public confidence as a proven instance of election or institutional interference.
“balance erosion” and “executive posture” turn respondents’ views into conclusions about what happened, rather than tagging the poll and its subject.

evidencebasis: The packet and latest descriptions report poll responses about whether checks and balances were working and distinguish perception from a legal finding. The PBS URL remains in source_urls.
notes: The title, medium, and long description report the result and its timing without claiming the poll proved a constitutional violation.

fieldissues.issue: “Oversight Was Running Behind Executive Momentum” asserts an oversight failure that the chronology does not establish.
The medium says oversight steps remain necessary to assess timing, which is internal analysis rather than a summary of the timeline.
The long description ends with “The supported event is,” an internal audit formulation, and it turns the short interval into a claim about oversight without describing any oversight failure.
“Election Interference” and “Democratic Institution Undermining” are not supported by the reported chronology.
The tags assert an oversight lag, legitimacy deficit, and urgency claim that the description does not establish.

proposedchanges.title: AP Timeline Traced Trump’s Iran Strike Decision From Talks to Air Force One
proposedchanges.description_short: AP Timeline Traced Trump’s Iran Strike Decision From Talks to Air Force One
proposedchanges.description_medium: AP’s March 2 timeline reported that Trump criticized Iran nuclear talks at 12:25 p.m. on February 27 and ordered a military operation at 3:38 p.m. while aboard Air Force One. U.S. and Israeli strikes began early February 28. The chronology shows a short interval, but does not establish that talks alone caused the decision or that no further consultation occurred.
proposedchanges.description_long: The Associated Press published a timeline on March 2 tracing Donald Trump’s decision to launch military action against Iran. On February 27, Trump said publicly that he was unhappy with nuclear negotiations and had not made a final decision. AP reported that he gave the strike order about three hours later, while aboard Air Force One. U.S. and Israeli attacks began early February 28 and killed Iran’s Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei and other senior officials, AP reported. The sequence documents a short interval between Trump’s remarks and the order, but it does not establish that dissatisfaction with negotiations alone caused the decision. Nor does it show that no military planning or consultation took place. The chronology links a diplomatic dispute to an imminent use of force, while leaving internal deliberations and other factors behind the order unspecified. AP’s timeline establishes the timing and reported outcome; it does not support the title’s implication that congressional or executive oversight lagged behind the decision.

evidencebasis: The packet and latest descriptions give the public comments, order time, Air Force One setting, and timing of the strikes. They do not establish an oversight failure or that talks alone caused the order. Both AP URLs remain in source_urls.
notes: The proposed copy retains the documented chronology while removing the unsupported oversight conclusion.

fieldissues.issue: “Carries Officer-Level Legal Jeopardy” can imply established liability or charges, while the long description says 17 incidents remained under investigation and no charges had been filed.
“Human Rights Violations” and “Public Welfare Harm” state an established violation or harm, while the report describes allegations under investigation.
“officer liability” and “legal jeopardy” imply a legal outcome that had not occurred; the tags also omit the investigation and named people.
The description names Mary Moriarty, Greg Bovino, Renee Good, and Alex Pretti, but the people tags include only Donald Trump.
The Hennepin County Attorney’s Office and Department of Homeland Security appear in the long description but are absent from organization tags.

proposedchanges.title: Minnesota Investigates Federal Immigration Officers Over 17 Incidents
proposedchanges.description_short: Minnesota Investigates Federal Immigration Officers Over 17 Incidents

evidencebasis: The latest long description identifies 17 alleged incidents, names the investigators and people involved, and states that no charges had been filed. It distinguishes allegations from findings. The AP URL remains in source_urls; the unrelated ProPublica URL is also retained from the packet.
notes: The medium and long descriptions already qualify the allegations and investigation status.

fieldissues.issue: “Fragile Archive Architecture Vulnerable to Trust Collapse” turns an unexplained disappearance count into a technical diagnosis and a predicted effect.
The medium calls the file count evidence of weak integrity controls and says it can undermine trust without evidence of cause or impact.

The long description repeatedly refers to the supplied account, notes, and rationale, and adds generic archive commentary instead of event detail. The packet does not identify the files, their dates of removal or restoration, or why they disappeared.
“Government Corruption” and “Transparency Obstruction” imply intentional misconduct, which the reported count does not establish.
The tags state technical weakness and trust collapse as conclusions rather than identifying the missing files and DOJ page.

proposedchanges.title: AP Reported at Least 16 Epstein Files Disappeared From DOJ Webpage
proposedchanges.description_short: AP Reported at Least 16 Epstein Files Disappeared From DOJ Webpage
proposedchanges.description_medium: On December 20, 2025, the Associated Press reported that at least 16 files had disappeared from the Justice Department webpage for documents related to Jeffrey Epstein. The report did not establish why the files were missing or whether they were later restored. The disappearance raised a question about the public release’s completeness, separate from the contents of the files.

evidencebasis: The packet and latest description establish only that AP reported at least 16 files absent from the DOJ webpage on December 20, 2025. They do not identify the files, explain the timing or cause, or state whether they returned. The AP URL remains in source_urls.
notes: A reader-facing 140–300 word explanation needs the file inventory or chronology and the DOJ’s explanation. The current packet does not supply those details, so a longer account would repeat the same uncertainty or add unsupported context.

fieldissues.issue: “Eliminating Emergency Lifesaving Treatment” says care was eliminated, while the event was rescission of federal guidance.

The long description says the action allowed hospitals to deny treatment, created a system of denial, violated EMTALA, and implemented Project 2025 without qualifying these claims. The medium only establishes that guidance was rescinded and that the ACLU said care remained at risk.
“lifesaving treatment denial,” “pregnant patient abandonment,” and “hospital refusal” present possible future effects as completed outcomes.
The long description names the ACLU, but organization_tags is empty.

proposedchanges.title: Trump Administration Rescinded EMTALA Emergency Abortion Guidance
proposedchanges.description_short: Trump Administration Rescinded EMTALA Emergency Abortion Guidance
proposedchanges.description_long:
On June 2, 2025, the Trump administration rescinded federal guidance on emergency abortion care under the Emergency Medical Treatment and Labor Act. The guidance had reaffirmed that hospitals receiving Medicare funds must provide health- or lifesaving abortion care to patients experiencing medical crises. The rescission removed that federal guidance about emergency care; it did not repeal EMTALA itself.

The action followed an anti-abortion group’s dismissal of its lawsuit challenging the protections. The ACLU said the rescission signaled that emergency abortion care remained at risk. That statement describes the organization’s concern, not evidence that hospitals had already denied care or that a particular patient had been harmed. The action concerned the administration’s guidance and enforcement posture.

The reports do not describe whether hospitals changed their decisions, whether patients lost access to care, or what effects followed the rescission. The ACLU warned that future emergency abortion care remained at risk, but the sources do not document a resulting denial of care.

evidencebasis: The packet’s medium documents the June 2 rescission, the guidance’s stated hospital obligations, the lawsuit dismissal, and the ACLU’s warning. The two packet URLs remain in source_urls.
notes: The revised title and long distinguish rescinded guidance from repeal of EMTALA or documented patient outcomes.
